content.title: About
content.content: Serrano pepper (Capsicum annuum) is a hot fresh pepper originally from Mexico. In this product the seeds have been removed and the fruit is intended to be eaten raw. It is bright green, 5–10 cm long, and has a characteristic fruity aroma with moderate heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Serrano is considered the “king” of Mexican peppers and is frequently used in salsa, guacamole, and hot sauces.
Its heat typically ranges from 2,000 to 2,500 Scoville Heat Units, making it moderately spicy.
Most of the capsaicin – the compound responsible for the burn – is concentrated in the seeds and inner membrane.
Serranos are grown both in greenhouses and open fields in warm climates.
In traditional Mexican cuisine the pepper is often dried to make chipotle.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Serrano peppers provide a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin has antioxidant properties, may boost metabolism, and can aid weight management.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in the pepper converts to vitamin A, essential for vision and skin health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Spicy foods stimulate gastric juice production, helping digestion.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Gastro‑intestinal irritation
items.content: People with sensitive stomachs may experience heartburn or irritation from hot peppers.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to capsaicin or other pepper components.

items.title: Caution with children
items.content: Due to its heat, only small amounts—or none at all—should be given to young children.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Capsaicin can enhance the effects of certain blood thinners; consult a doctor if you take such medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Seeded serrano can be added to salads, salsas, marinades, soups, and sandwiches. It is often sliced into thin rings or finely chopped. Soaking in cold water for 10–15 minutes can reduce the heat if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh serrano peppers in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, placed in a perforated bag. They stay fresh for 1–2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze sliced pieces in an airtight bag.
